newsitem.title: USA: Key from alley rental-truck type, bomb trial hears.
newsitem.headline: Key from alley rental-truck type, bomb trial hears.

text.p: A lock expert testified Tuesday that a key found near the bombed-out Oklahoma City federal building fit the type of truck the government alleges Timothy McVeigh used to carry the bomb.

Prosecutors revealed for the first time Tuesday during questioning that a key had been found in an alley a few blocks from the Alfred P. Murrah federal building three days after the blast that killed 168 people on April 19, 1995.

Star prosecution witness Michael Fortier testified Monday that McVeigh had told him months earlier he planned to park a getaway car in the alley behind the YMCA building, a few blocks from the bomb site.

In Tuesday's testimony, lock expert Charles Edwards identified the key as a Ford 10-bit without the company's logotype -- a normal feature of keys that Ford sells such fleet customers as rental companies.

In 1996 the FBI sent Edwards specifications of a type of lock used in some 1993 Ford F-700 trucks and asked him to make a lock and key of that type. The government has said that the truck used in the bombing was a Ryder truck made by Ford.
In a dramatic end to the day's testimony, Edwards said he had recently tried out the key that investigators found at the scene in the lock he made and that it worked.
"Did you try the lock?" prosecutor Aitan Goelman asked. "What did you find?"
"That key functioned in the locks that I built," Edwards replied.

Prosecutors also presented videotape showing a blue pickup truck with a camper shell top taken three days before the bombing by a security camera at the Regency Towers apartment building a block from the Murrah federal building.

The government has claimed that alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols drove his dark blue pickup GMC truck with a white camper shell to Oklahoma City on April 16, 1995, three days before the bombing, to help McVeigh drop off his getaway car. Nichols will be tried separately later.

William Stokes, who heads the FBI laboratory's photographic operations, testified that he believed the security videotape also captured a 20-foot Ford Ryder truck going by the building on the day of the bombing.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty to the bombing. If convicted, he faces the death penalty.
The key and security tape testimony was presented after the prosecution's star witness, Fortier, underwent a round of cross-examination by McVeigh's chief attorney, Stephen Jones.

Jones tried to portray McVeigh's former Army buddy as a drug user who could not be trusted. But Fortier, 28, kept his composure as Jones attacked his credibility and portrayed him as someone who had been coached by prosecutors and who was desperate to save his own skin.

"I don't think they poked many holes in the core of his testimony," Andrew Cohen, an attorney who is analysing the trial for CBS News, said. "What they did was try to poke holes in him as a person who would give honest testimony. Instead of trying to attack the message, you try to kill the messenger."
Fortier had testified that McVeigh planned the bombing to avenge a government siege at Waco, Texas, two years earlier and spark an uprising among the American people.

Fortier pleaded guilty to four felony counts, including knowing about a felony and failing to report it, in return for testifying that he knew about plans for the bombing but did nothing to stop it. Now in federal prison awaiting sentencing, he faces a term of up to 23 years.
